The house on the shore had been empty for years, and they broke in through a window with the salt still drying on their arms. Tobias remembered the beach party only as noise behind them; Ivy remembered the way the floorboards gave. It was the end of the rail line, the last stop, and after that there was nothing but water.

Two years of it. The frozen river where she walked out farther than he dared and stood laughing on the ice. The noodle house with the cracked lantern where she ate his egg too. The drive-in in October, heater roaring, the film forgotten. Then the slow curdling: her breath sweet with gin at four in the afternoon, his silences long as corridors, both of them expert now at the small precise wound. The last night she came home with his fender crumpled and her keys in her fist and said things neither of them could take back, and then she walked out, and that was the end of it.

He didn't know about the clinic until he went to the bookshop where she worked and she looked at him with a stranger's polite patience and turned back to a young man with a cheap haircut, laughing, touching his wrist. Peck, his name tag said.

Nina and Grady sat him down with the form letter. *Ivy Marsh has had you erased. Please do not attempt to contact her.* He read it four times and then drove to Lacuna and stood in front of Dr. Hallam and said, do it to me, do the same thing.

They gave him a box. Every object: the ticket stubs, the chipped bowl, the record she'd scratched, her toothbrush, a shell from the shore. He held each one while a machine drew the map of where it lived in him.

The technicians came at midnight — Dell, who called him chief, and Peck, who pocketed the shell and the stubs while Tobias lay unconscious with wires in his hair.

Inside, Tobias walked backward through his own house. The fight went first, dissolving wall by wall, her voice thinning to nothing. Then the recriminations, the slammed doors, the empty bottles going out like candles. He let them go gladly. But then he was in the noodle house with the lantern, and she was reaching for his egg, and he understood what he had bargained away. He began to run. He carried her into places she had never been — his childhood kitchen, the school gym, under the table where he'd hidden aged four — hiding her behind curtains, folding her into rooms the map didn't cover.

In the flat, Dell and Rosa the receptionist smoked on his bed and watched the readouts go wild without seeing them. When Hallam arrived to re-map, Rosa kissed him in the hallway, and his wife, waiting in the car, told her flatly that whatever had happened between Rosa and Hallam had been taken out of her months ago, and she'd signed for it herself.

The last room left was the empty house on the shore. The walls were going. Ivy stood in the salt light and said, so this is it, and he said yes, and she said: meet me at the beach. Then nothing.

He woke to grey morning, alone, a headache and no reason for it. At the station he stood on the platform and did not go to work. He bought a ticket to the coast because his hands did it. Ivy was on the frozen sand in a red coat, having come for reasons she also couldn't name, and they looked at each other like people who had misplaced something.

They drove back to the city talking about nothing, and she said, do you want to come up.

Rosa, who had cleared out her desk that week, mailed every file and every tape to every name on the books.

So they sat on Ivy's floor with a cassette player between them and heard their own voices flay each other, patient, expert, unforgivable. Ivy got up and left. Tobias stayed where he was. Ten minutes later she was in the doorway, coat still on, and she said, okay.

He said, okay.

The snow came sideways off the ridge that winter, and in the boarding house kitchen Emmett Rusk's mother put her name to a paper that gave her son to a banker. A lodger had run out on his rent and left behind a deed to a hole in the mountain, and the hole had turned out to be worth a fortune, and the fortune had turned out to be worth a boy. Barrow stood in the doorway in his city coat. Outside the boy came down the slope on his sled with his whole small weight behind it and drove the runners into Barrow's stomach, and Barrow wheezed, and the mother said his name once, and by nightfall the boy was on a train going east, and his parents were not.

On his twenty-fifth birthday he took the fortune out of Barrow's hands. Barrow read him the list: mines, timber, railroad shares, ships, and, at the bottom, a small failing newspaper in a river city, valued at nothing. "That one," Emmett said. "I want to run the Clarion."

He moved into the building itself, sleeping on a cot behind the composing room. He brought in Marsh to keep the books and Devlin to write, and on the front page he printed a signed statement of principles, in which he promised the working people of the city a paper that would tell them the truth without fear. Devlin cut it out and kept it. Within a year Emmett had hired away every reporter, editor, and photographer of the rival paper across the street, and he gave a party for them with a brass band and a chorus line and himself dancing in the middle of it with his collar open.

He went abroad to buy statues and came home engaged to Adele, the governor's niece. There were breakfasts. In the first she leaned toward him laughing; in the tenth they sat at opposite ends of a lengthening table behind separate newspapers, and the only sound was paper.

He met Nora Kell on a street corner with mud on his coat, a shopgirl who laughed at him for it, and he began going to her rooms in the evenings and telling nobody. In the middle of his campaign for governor the party boss Halloran brought Adele up those narrow stairs and stood in Nora's parlor and offered him a choice: withdraw, or be printed. Emmett said he would not withdraw. He lost by ninety thousand votes. Devlin asked to be transferred to the paper in another city, and Emmett granted it, and Adele took the divorce and went home to her uncle.

He married Nora and decided she would sing opera. She had no voice. He built her a teacher, a stage, an orchestra; on the night of her debut the audience coughed through the second act, and in the Clarion office a drunk Devlin began the review, calling it a shameful evening, and fell asleep over his typewriter. Emmett read the half page, finished it in the same savage vein, sent it to the presses, and fired Devlin in the morning. Nora swallowed poison rather than sing again, and while she lay grey in the bed he said, all right, all right, no more.

He shut her away in the unfinished palace on the hill he called Silvermount, among crates of statuary, and she worked jigsaw puzzles on the floor of a hall so vast the fire could not warm it. After a picnic at the shore where nobody spoke and a quarrel that lasted three sentences, she packed her cases and went. He wrecked her bedroom, tore the hangings, broke the glass, and then stopped, holding a small glass globe with snow inside it, and murmured, "Bluebell," and carried it out past the endless mirrors, each one giving him back smaller.

He died alone there with that word on his lips, and the globe rolled from his hand and broke on the floor.

The newsreel recited the mines, the papers, the campaign, the palace, and ended without explaining the word. So Nash was sent. A drunk Nora turned him out of a seaside nightclub. He read Barrow's memoir, and sat with Marsh, and with Devlin, who still had the statement of principles, and at last with Nora, and with Colm the butler, who had heard the word and thought nothing of it.

"No one word explains a life," Nash said in the great hall, while below them workmen shoveled the leavings into the furnace: crates, canvases, and a child's sled with BLUEBELL painted along its side.

The first thing I know is the ceiling of a motel room I do not remember renting, and a phone against my ear, and my own voice telling a stranger about Elias Prine.

I say: I was an investigator. I sat across a table from a man who claimed he could not hold a new minute in his head, and I wrote that his damage was in his mind, not his brain, and the company kept its money. I say: his wife was diabetic. She did not believe him either. She held out her arm and asked for her insulin, and then asked again, and again, testing him, and he loved her enough to give her every dose she asked for, and she died on the kitchen floor while he stood there believing he had just come in from the yard.

The caller listens. The caller always listens. Then he gives me a name — Gil Marsh, dealer, and an address — and I write it on the back of a photograph because writing is the only thing I have that outlasts me.

Here are the facts inked on my body. There were two men in our bathroom. I killed one of them with my hands. The other put something into the side of my skull and took away my capacity to keep anything, including her. His initials are R.M. That is fact five. I burned her hairbrush and her books in a field once, I have a photo of the smoke, and I remember nothing of grieving, only that the picture makes my chest hurt for as long as I am looking at it.

The basement is derelict, wet concrete, a mattress rotting in the corner. Gil Marsh is heavier than I expect and slower than he thinks. I hit him until he stops shaping words, and then I put my forearm across his throat and hold it, and just before he goes he whispers something that sounds like Elias. I write it down. I will never know what it meant. I photograph his face and shake the picture dry. His suit fits me. His sports car starts on the first turn.

A plainclothes cop named Roy finds me in the parking lot. He has a face I have apparently trusted before; there is a Polaroid of him in my jacket. He says Gil was nobody, Gil was a hustler who sold to teenagers, Gil didn't touch your wife. He says: I helped you find the real one, a year ago, in a place like that basement, and you killed him, and twenty minutes later you asked me where he was. He says: there was no claimant. You are the man in that story. Your wife tested you and you killed her with kindness, one shot at a time, and you invented Prine so you could keep on being the man who denied him.

I look at his mouth moving and I burn Gil's photographs in the ashtray of a stolen car. On the back of Roy's picture I write *he is lying to you*. I copy his licence plate onto my palm and drive to a parlour where a man with tired eyes needles it into my thigh, the sixth fact, permanent as scripture.

At a bar out on the highway, a woman goes white when she sees the suit and the car through the window. Her name is Corinne. She brings me a beer that the kitchen has spat in and watches me drink it. Later, in her house, there is not a single pen anywhere, not one, and she says things about my wife until I hit her, and then she leaves and comes back with her eye swollen shut, weeping, saying a man called Vance did it. So I wait in a motel bathroom and break Vance's nose against the sink and put a gun in his ribs and drive him twenty miles out and leave him walking.

Corinne knows a girl at the vehicle registry. She lays the printout on the table like a gift: the plate, the name. Roy Mercer.

R.M.

I ask him to meet me at the derelict building. He talks the whole way down the stairs, patient, gentle, saying my name. I shoot him through the head and take his picture and write on it, so that I will know, so that I will finally be able to stop.

I have such a good feeling about this one.

The soldier came home thin as a rail and knelt down in front of the boy on the porch, and out of his fist came a gold watch, warm from being carried in places no one would look. Your father wanted you to have this, he said. The boy, Denny, was seven. He kept it for thirty years.

Rollo drove and Marcus talked. In Denmark, Rollo said, they'll sell you the stuff right out of a window, no fuss, and nobody says a word about it. And they don't call a milkshake a milkshake, they call it something else entirely. What do they call it, said Marcus. I forget, said Rollo.

Outside the flat they waited in the corridor, and Rollo said a foot massage was nothing, and Marcus said a man's wife's foot is a man's wife's foot, and Rollo said you don't throw somebody off a balcony over toes. Then Marcus knocked. Inside, a young man named Tobin sat on a sofa with a briefcase that did not belong to him, and Marcus recited the passage about the path of the righteous and the tyranny of evil men, and then they shot him. As they gathered the case, a fourth man burst out of the bathroom and emptied a revolver at them from six feet away and hit neither of them, only plaster. That, Marcus said afterward, was God coming down and stopping the bullets. Rollo said it was a bad shot.

In the car Rollo turned around to ask their passenger Del what he thought about it and the gun went off and Del's head went away. They drove with the windows down, dripping, to Warren's house, where Warren stood in his dressing gown saying not in my garage, and a fixer arrived in a dinner jacket with a stopwatch and told them where to scrub, and hosed them both down in the yard, and gave them T-shirts and shorts so they looked like tourists.

Elsewhere that morning two small-time robbers sat over eggs and coffee, and the woman said liquor stores were finished, and the man looked around at the register and the tips and said this place, right now, and she screamed and they stood up on the seats. Marcus was in the booth with the briefcase. He talked to the man very quietly with his hand on his own gun and gave him his wallet from his own pocket and told him to take the money and leave the case, because the case belonged to somebody, and he let the two of them walk out the door with their bag full of billfolds.

They brought the case to Otis at his bar, where Otis was counting notes into the hands of an ageing boxer named Denny and saying: the fifth. You go down in the fifth.

Rollo bought his heroin from Kip that evening and shot up in Kip's kitchen before taking Otis's wife Nadia out to a diner where the waiters dressed as dead film stars, and they won the dance contest barefoot. Back at the house she found the packet in his coat, thought it was cocaine, snorted it, and went down foaming. Rollo drove her to Kip's, and Kip found the adrenaline and the medical book, and they knelt on the living-room carpet and drove the needle into her heart, and she sat up screaming and alive.

Denny did not go down in the fifth. He won, and the other man died on the canvas from it, and Denny went out a side door and into a taxi in his robe. In a motel across town his girlfriend Marielle had packed everything except the watch, and when he understood that, something in him stopped working. He went back to the flat. There was a submachine gun lying on the kitchen counter and Rollo came out of the bathroom, and Denny picked it up and killed him, and put the watch on his wrist, and left.

Two streets away he hit Otis with the car. They woke tied up in a pawnshop basement, and the men who owned that basement took Otis into the back room. Denny worked his ropes loose, went up, came down again with a sword off the wall, and finished it. Otis, ruined and quiet, said they were square if Denny left town forever.

Denny took a motorcycle from the shop floor, collected Marielle, and rode out through morning traffic.

Pruitt made him tell it eleven times in a parked car that smelled of old coffee.

"Again," Pruitt said. "But don't perform it. Remember it."

So Danny Roarke told it again: the public toilet on Fenn Street, the dealer with a kilo in a carrier bag sitting on the cistern, the two of them wedged in a stall while a school group filed past outside. By the eleventh telling he could smell the disinfectant. That was the trick. You didn't lie. You remembered something that never happened.

He told it in a back room three days later to an old man with a cardigan and a butcher's hands, and the old man's son, and a lean quiet one called Mr. Ash. Bram listened with his chin down. Cal laughed in the right place, which was the wrong place. Ash didn't laugh at all, but afterward he put a hand on Danny's shoulder, and Danny understood that he was in.

"You'll be Mr. Elm," Bram said later, dealing out names like cards. "Ash. Cedar. Birch."

"Why do I get Birch?" said Birch. "Birch is a girl's tree. Give me Cedar. Cedar's got weight."

"You get what you get," Bram said.

Ren Vasco came to them straight from the gates, four years thinner, and Bram embraced him and Cal poured him a drink because they owed him those four years of silence. Vasco drank it like water.

At breakfast the morning of, they argued about a song on the radio, whether it was about a woman or about heroin, and then about whether the waitress had earned four percent or nothing at all. Elm put a note under his saucer when nobody was looking, and Ash saw him do it, and said nothing.

The job died in under a minute. Alarms already ringing when they crossed the marble. Uniforms on the street like they'd been standing there since dawn. Ash drove with one hand and fired out the window with the other, and Elm hunched in the passenger seat shouting directions he was making up.

They split on foot. Elm dragged a man out of a hatchback at a junction, and the man — sixty, cardigan, terrified, a hero for four seconds — put a small revolver into Elm's stomach and fired. For three years I did not sleep. I investigated recalls for an automotive firm — I calculated whether it was cheaper to fix the steering column or settle with the families — and at night I lay in my catalogue bed and stared at the ceiling like a man watching a blank screen for a picture.

The cure was accidental. I wandered into a support group for men with testicular cancer and someone held me against his chest and I wept until my ribs hurt, and that night I slept like earth. So I collected diseases I did not have. Blood parasites. Ascending bowel cancer. Tuesdays, brain tumours. I was healthy in the way a tourist is local.

Then Ada Vey came. She sat with a cigarette behind her ear and lied through every round of sharing, and because she was faking I could see that I was faking, and the crying stopped working, and the sleep went with it.

On a flight to Dayton I sat beside a man in a red leather jacket who sold soap and talked about the way a coffee table can eat a life. Rex Marrow. I put his card in my pocket without deciding to.

My flat came apart while I was in the air. Gas, they said. My sofa, my lamps with unpronounceable names, my dishes shaped like sincerity, all of it went out the fifteenth-floor window in pieces. I stood in a phone booth in the rain and called Rex, and he took me to a house at the edge of the industrial district, a leaning wooden thing with rain coming through the roof and worms in the wet plaster.

Outside a bar, after, he asked me to hit him as hard as I could. I hit his ear. He hit my ribs. We rolled on the wet asphalt of the car park laughing with blood on our teeth, and I slept nine hours.

Other men wanted it. In the basement under the bar we made rules: two men to a fight, no shirts, no shoes, no questions afterward. Every week there were more. I went to work with a split lip and a face like a boiled fruit, and when the director threatened me I bled on his carpet and threw myself down and screamed until security came, and he paid me a salary to stay away from the building. Rex called it corporate sponsorship.

Ada swallowed a bottle of pills and phoned the house, and Rex went and got her, and then for months I lay listening to the two of them through the wall, hating the ceiling.

Rex stole liposuction fat from the clinic behind the mall and rendered it in the kitchen with lye and sold the bars back to the department stores at eighty dollars each. Selling rich women their own fat, he said. One night he poured lye on the back of my hand and held my wrist while it burned and would not let me go somewhere else in my head. Stay here, he said. This is the greatest moment of your life.

Havoc came after that: shaven heads sleeping in rows on the floorboards, taking orders, ruining corporate art and burning franchise coffee. He drove us into oncoming headlights, let the car roll into the ditch, and afterward he was simply gone.

Then a man called Ogden was shot on an operation, and I began trying to shut it down. City to city I found basements already running, and men who looked at my swollen face and said, Welcome back, Mr Marrow.

I understood in a motel in Tulsa. There was no Rex. There was only me, walking and talking and building an army while my body pretended to sleep. Ada said it flatly on the phone: it was you, it has always been you.

Havoc had mined the towers of the debt-record companies. I went down into the garages to pull the fuses and he came out of the dark and beat me down a stairwell, and at the top I put the gun in my own mouth and fired through my cheek, and he was not there anymore.

They brought Ada up to me, gently, and we stood at the window holding hands while the buildings folded into the street below.

The cardiologist gave him weeks. Aaron Vale, who had spent his life proving things that could not be disproved, listened to the numbers and found them elegant and unanswerable. Della came to the apartment she had left two years before and sat with her coat on. "There's sperm frozen in a clinic in Rockville," she said. "Sign the release. Let me have something." He signed, because it cost him nothing, or he thought it cost him nothing.

Across town, in a house with a chain-link yard, Wes Tarrow rose at five to be at the loading dock by six, and on Saturdays he stood behind a backstop yelling grace at eleven-year-olds. He had been in prison for four years and saved for one. Nita watched him read scripture with his thumb pressed white against the page and thought: he has only changed the direction of the burning.

Lena Ward had been clean nine years. She had Doug, who checked the tire pressure on both cars every month, and Ellie and June, who slept in the same bed although each had her own.

It was a Tuesday. Doug walked the girls to the crossing at Ferris and Ninth. Wes's pickup came through the light and took all three of them; he drove two blocks, turned around, came back far enough to see what was in the road, and then he ran. At the hospital a doctor said husband, said both, and Lena heard the plural and understood that there was nothing left to be careful for.

Doug's heart went into Aaron Vale's chest that same night. He woke to a sensation he had forgotten, a steady animal knocking, and he wept in front of strangers.

Four days later Wes walked into a police station on Delmar and said the words and went back inside.

Lena found a dealer within a week. She did it the way she did everything, thoroughly, on schedule, as though destroying herself were a job Doug had left unfinished.

Aaron went home and could not stop the question. Whose. He hired an investigator, a tired man named Pauling, and paid him in cash, and three weeks later held a page with a name and an address and a photograph taken through a windshield. He learned she swam at the Y on Thursdays. He arranged to be in the next lane, to be clumsy, to apologize. Her wrists were thin as pencils. She let him buy her coffee, and then let him into the wreck of her house, and neither of them pretended it was kindness.

He told Della he was leaving. She stood in the kitchen with a chart of her cycles on the refrigerator. "I don't want the child," he said. "I don't want any of it." She did not throw anything, which was worse.

It was a Sunday when he told Lena about the heart. She hit him once, flat-handed, and put him out on the step in the rain, and at two in the morning she opened the door and pulled him inside by the shirt and pressed her ear to his chest for an hour without speaking.

Wes came out early for good behavior. He stood in his own doorway with his bag still in his hand and told Nita he was finished, with her, with the church, with pretending a man could be forgiven, and he took a job changing sheets at a motel three hundred miles south.

"Kill him," Lena said. Not loudly. She said it while cutting a peach. Aaron bought a revolver from a man in a parking lot and drove south with Lena asleep against the window.

He found the room. He found Wes sitting on the bed with the TV on. His hand shook so badly the bullet went through the meat of Wes's thigh, and Aaron said, absurdly, "Run. Please run."

Wes did not run. He tied his leg with a pillowcase and followed the car and knocked on their door at dawn and stood there bleeding and said, "Finish it. I'm asking you." Lena was in the doorway. Aaron looked at the two of them, and at the whole ledger, and put the barrel under his own jaw.

They carried him between them. In the corridor a nurse said the transplanted heart had failed, and Lena laughed once, a terrible sound.

Wes drove north and went home to Nita. Lena went home alone, seven weeks pregnant, and shut the door.

The house held five and a half people: his mother, Nestor, Alma, the baby, and Ruben on a mattress by the kitchen where he could hear everything. He heard the pharmacy job being planned in whispers, and later the sound of Nestor's hand against Alma's face, which was flatter and quieter than people imagine. Afterward he would find her in the yard and say, *come with me, we'll go tonight, I have money*, and she would look at the baby's mouth and say nothing.

It was in the yard that he learned what Tigre was. The rottweiler took a neighbour's dog by the throat without hurrying, the way a man closes a door. Ruben started walking him to the lots behind the tannery where they fought dogs on Sundays, and Tigre won, and won, and Ruben rolled the bills into a sock inside the wall.

He paid two men from the bus terminal to break Nestor's ribs. It cost him almost nothing and it cost him everything: Nestor came home limping, and by morning he was gone, and Alma was gone, and the baby, and the sock in the wall.

Across the city, Celine Vaz stood at her new window looking at her own face forty feet high on the billboard opposite, cigarettes she didn't smoke, and Hector behind her saying he had told his wife, told the girls, it was done. Her lapdog Chispa turned circles on the unfamiliar parquet.

Tigre's last fight ended when Chaco the promoter, having bet wrong, shot him in the ribs in the middle of the ring. Ruben went over the barrier and put a knife into Chaco twice, and then Pipo had him by the collar, and then they were in the car with the dog bleeding across the back seat, and then the red light at the junction of Bernal and the avenue, and Ruben went through it at eighty.

Cardo was standing at that corner with a plastic bag of bread. He had been a guerrilla once and now he killed men for money and slept among dogs. He watched the two cars fold into each other, watched the woman's white leg wedged under the dashboard, and then he heard something moving in the wreck and pulled out the rottweiler by the loose skin of its neck and carried it away before the ambulances came.

Celine woke with her femur pinned like a hem. Somewhere in the flat, Chispa had gone through a gap in the floorboards, and Hector tore up the parquet room by room, calling into the dark under the house, while the bone went bad above her knee. They took the leg on a Thursday. The following month a crane lifted her face off the billboard and the frame stood empty for a long time.

Nestor was shot dead going out of a bank on Rivadavia. At the funeral Ruben stood beside Alma and said it one last time, *come with me*, and she said no, and it was not even a hard no; it was tired.

Cardo fed the dog by hand, chewed meat, warm milk, and Tigre healed among the strays in his yard. Then Elian came with an envelope and a name: Sergio, his half-brother, his partner, forty per cent.

The week Cardo went to watch his wife buried from behind a wall of jasmine, he followed the grown woman in black who had her mouth—Perla—home to a fourth-floor flat with geraniums. He wrote down the address.

He came back to find every dog in his yard dead and Tigre sitting among them, mildly, tail moving. Cardo put the barrel against the flat skull and held it there a long time and then lowered it and sat down on the ground and wept without noise.

He took Sergio easily and chained him to a pipe instead of killing him. He fed him. Then he drove Elian out to the lair and sat the brothers facing each other, and laid a loaded pistol on the concrete exactly between them, and walked out with both their money.

He broke Perla's lock, spoke twenty minutes into her answering machine—his name, her mother, the years, the men, everything—and took her photograph from the shelf.

Then he shaved, bathed, put on a clean shirt, left the money stacked on her kitchen table, and walked out past the last houses into the wasteland with Tigre limping at his knee.

The gun dealer laughed at the way Nadir said *revolver*, drawing the syllables out like taffy, and Sahar signed the paperwork with her jaw set, because her father's hands were shaking too badly to hold a pen.

That same evening, outside a restaurant with valet stands and heat lamps, Trey put a pistol in the prosecutor Halstead's ribs while Kwame took the keys, and they drove off laughing about how the man had said *please* twice.

North of there, Officer Boyle leaned into a stopped car and ran his hand up Renee Hobart's thigh while her husband Clay stood on the curb with his fists closed and his mouth closed too, and afterward Boyle said, *Just a warning tonight, folks.* In the morning Voss stood in the commander's doorway and asked for his own car. The commander asked if he had a reason he could write down. Voss said he'd rather not ride with a racist, and the commander wrote *flatulence*.

Mateo rekeyed the Halsteads' front door while Paula stood at the top of the stairs telling her husband, loudly, that the man with the tattoo would sell their keys to his *homies* by dawn. Mateo left the invoice on the counter and drove to Nadir's shop, where he put in a new deadbolt and said, *The lock is fine, but the door is broken, you need a new door.* Nadir heard a hustle, an upsell, a con, and shouted until Mateo tore up the ticket and left.

Boyle spent his lunch hour in a beige office begging a clerk named Delia Frank to approve a specialist for his father, who could not urinate without weeping. She said the plan didn't cover it. He said her name, twice, like a threat, and she said his name back, and nothing changed.

The shop was smashed that night, shelves swept, register gone, and the insurance adjuster circled the words *failure to remedy known defect* and refused to pay a cent.

Renee Hobart hung upside down in a folded car with gasoline running toward her hair, screaming at the officer who reached in that she didn't want him, not him, and Boyle crawled through broken glass into the smell of fuel and dragged her out onto the asphalt as the thing went up behind them.

Trey and Kwame hit a shopkeeper named Pham with a stolen car, wedged him under the bumper, and dumped him bleeding at a hospital driveway because Kwame couldn't stop hearing him breathe.

Clay Hobart, trying to get his own car back from a garage that had impounded it, was surrounded mid-reach by four officers with guns drawn, and it was Voss who stepped in front of the barrels saying *he lives there, he lives there,* until they let the man stand up. Later Clay drove Trey out of a police chase at ninety miles an hour, said nothing the whole way, and then reached across, opened the door, and put him out on the shoulder.

Nadir sat in his truck outside Mateo's house until Mateo came up the walk, and he raised the gun and Rosie came running out the screen door, arms up, *Papa*, into her father's chest, and Nadir fired.

The dream came again, she told him, the red tunnel, walls slick and breathing, and no end to it. Cort lay with his hand flat between her shoulder blades and said it was Jonah's flat she was dreaming of, that awful red carpet, and Lise laughed into the pillow and said Jonah had better taste than to keep a man like him around. Cort said Jonah had no taste at all, look who he'd let go. She said mind yourself. The window was open and the street below made its small noises.

Two mornings later she sat on the edge of the bath with the flat empty around her and watched the second line arrive, faint and then not faint, and she did not move for a long time.

In the afternoon she took a book to the park. The sprinklers went round with their tick and hiss, and children ran shrieking through them and out again, hair flattened to their skulls. She read four pages in an hour. Her free hand lay across her stomach, not pressing, just resting there the way a hand rests on a sleeping animal.

On the underground to the party the three of them held the rail and argued. Jonah said men thought about it more; Lise said men only talked about it more, which was not the same thing, and Cort said he could prove it either way given a drink. She said that was the problem, given a drink. Jonah laughed. Cort said he was celebrating. She hadn't told him what.

By eleven he had passed through cheerful and out the other side. She watched him take something in the kitchen from a girl with silver rings on every finger, watched him lean into her neck and say something that made the girl put a hand on his chest, and then watched him do it again to somebody else. Lise found her jacket under a pile of coats and left without saying goodbye to anyone.

The road outside was four lanes and moving. Rather than wait for the lights she took the underpass, and halfway down the tiled stairs she heard it — the sound of a fist and a woman crying, and she came round the turn into a strip light and a man in a long coat holding a woman by the hair. She was tall, with a torn dress, mascara down to her jaw. The man was known on that stretch as the Adder. He looked at Lise the way a dog looks up from a bowl.

Afterwards she remembered the ceiling of the tunnel, the pipes, the concrete taking the back of her head again and again. Someone came to the bottom of the stairs — a man with a jacket over his arm — and stood there a half second, and then his shoes went back up the way they'd come.

Cort came out of the party at two with Jonah behind him, both of them squinting, and there were blue lights on the wet road and a stretcher going up into an ambulance, and a paramedic's arm across Cort's chest, and Cort making a sound neither of them recognised.

Two men were smoking at the corner. They knew the name, they said, and the name had a price, and once the notes had changed hands they gave it and said try the Pit, he drinks there. Cort went through that club like a man going through a house on fire, table to table, and grabbed a shaven-headed man by the collar, and the man took his arm at the elbow and turned it until it broke with a sound like a chair leg. Cort went down. Jonah pulled the fire extinguisher off the wall and swung it, and swung it, and kept swinging until the face was not a face, while four feet away a man in a long coat watched with his drink held at his chest and did not put it down.

The police came in and knelt on both of them and put the cuffs on and carried them out into the street, Cort's broken arm hanging, Jonah's shoes squeaking on the tile, the doorway full of phone lights.

In a flat above that street, an old man stood at the window with his back to a younger one and said: nothing lasts, you understand. Not the guilty, not the wronged, not the stone they're broken on. Time takes it all. Give it long enough and there is no tunnel and no one in it.

They came out of the diamond house in the northern port in long black coats and wide black hats, beards to the chest, singing softly, and no one looked twice at four pilgrims on a Friday afternoon. Solly Two Coats carried the stone in his fist like a boiled sweet. That night his cousin Marv rang from overseas and said bring it straight over, don't stop, don't breathe, don't get clever.

Solly stopped. Solly got clever. He always did.

It was Grigor the Nail who told him about the bookmaker's off the high street, warm as a bath, good odds on the fight, and it was Grigor the Nail who mentioned to Ike and Benno, pawnbrokers by trade and thieves by nature, that a man with a case would be sitting in that same bookmaker's at half seven.

Meanwhile, across town, Halloway and Digby, promoters of pugilism, sent Pretty Sam out to a travellers' camp to buy a caravan cheap. There was a disagreement about the price. A bare-knuckle man named Finn settled it with one left hand, and Pretty Sam went to sleep in the mud with his good looks rearranged, which left Halloway a man short for a bout he had already sold to Coldstone. So Halloway put Finn in instead and swore on his mother's grave that Finn would lie down in the fourth.

Solly landed, took a taxi to Hersch the fence, handed over the stone for counting, and walked into the bookmaker's with an empty case and a full heart. Ike, Benno and Tulley came through the door like a bag of spanners falling downstairs. There was shouting, there was a machete that Ike had bought for atmosphere, and there was Solly's arm, still holding the handle, going out the door in a carrier bag. Grigor came in the back and chased them off, firing at their tyres and missing.

In the ring that night Finn looked at the fourth round, decided he didn't fancy waiting, and put his opponent to sleep in the first. Coldstone lost a fortune and took it out of Halloway's face with a telephone.

Marv flew in the next morning, found Solly's hotel room empty and his cousin absent, and hired Ledge, who found people for money and had never yet failed to. Grigor found Solly first, in a lock-up, and cut the rest of the arm away to get the case open, which was a great deal of work for a case containing a passport, a sandwich and no diamond at all.

Ledge traced the pawnbrokers to a car park, shot their car into scrap metal, and drove away with Ike and Benno in the back and the stone in his pocket, because Hersch's people had been careless and it had passed through three sets of hands since Tuesday.

Coldstone fed Solly to his pigs and explained to Halloway and Digby, over the sound of eating, exactly what would happen to them if the second fight went the wrong way. They went to Finn and told him: down in the fourth, son, it isn't a request. That night Coldstone's men set fire to Finn's mother's caravan with her inside it, to make certain.

Grigor ambushed Ledge on a back road with a shotgun and good intentions. When the smoke lifted, Ledge was dead, Grigor was dead, Benno was dead in the footwell, and Tulley, who had been hiding behind a hedge for an hour, walked away with nothing but a lurcher that had eaten something shiny off the road.

Finn came out for the fourth round and knocked his opponent unconscious with a right hand you could hear in the car park. Then the travellers rose out of the crowd with hammers and chains and went through Coldstone's men like weather. Halloway and Digby found Coldstone under the seating, blubbering, and shot him twice, once each, so as to share it. By morning the camp was gone, every wheel of it, the grass still flat where it had been.

A fortnight later a lurcher was handed in at a pet shop with a bad stomach, coughed once on the lino, and produced the biggest diamond in the north of Europe. Which is how Halloway and Digby came to be standing in a pet shop, holding it, looking at each other, saying nothing at all.

The party was Emlyn's, of course. They were always Emlyn's, and Wilder was always the first to arrive and the last to leave, because that was the shape of a friendship twenty years old. Downstairs the guests were working through the gin. Upstairs, on the landing where the coats were piled, Wilder put his hand flat against the wall beside Odile's head and told her she was the loveliest woman in the house, which was true, and that he had thought so for six years, which was also true.

They took rooms in a district nobody they knew had reason to visit — two rooms above a dry cleaner's, with a gas fire that had to be coaxed. Within a month they had bought linen, and then plates, and then a set of small green cups Odile found in a junk shop, and by summer the affair had a household of its own, more thoroughly furnished than most marriages. They kept salt there. They kept a corkscrew and a spare pair of Wilder's socks.

In October she told him she was pregnant, and that it was Emlyn's, and neither of them suggested that anything should change. Tuesdays and Fridays, as before. She washed the green cups afterwards and set them upside down on the draining board.

Abroad the following spring, in a hotel in Cadiz with a ceiling fan and a bad view, Emlyn came up from the desk holding a letter and asked, quite pleasantly, whether she was expecting anything from Wilder, because the hand on the envelope was one he'd known since school. She had prepared no defence and offered none. She simply told him, at some length, standing by the window with her arms folded.

Emlyn heard her out. Then he said that she should understand something, which was that he had always been fonder of Wilder than of her, and had never pretended otherwise to himself, and he supposed this altered the arithmetic in ways she might not have anticipated. He rang down for coffee. They stayed the remaining nine days and swam.

She came back and went up the stairs above the dry cleaner's on the Friday and said nothing at all about Spain. The gas fire was coaxed. The afternoon passed exactly as the others had passed.

In June the two men had lunch at a restaurant off the Strand that ran three hours. Emlyn drank most of a second bottle and baited Wilder about contemporary fiction — the sentences like wet string, the prizes, the young men writing about their fathers — and Wilder defended his list and enjoyed himself enormously, and Emlyn never once said the word Cadiz. In September, at dinner in Emlyn and Odile's dining room, the two of them discussed squash, then rackets, then a housemaster's forehand in 1961, for an hour and forty minutes, until Odile sat between them with nothing whatever to say and understood that she had been placed somewhere outside the conversation permanently.

The rooms became a chore before the child was two. It was a Tuesday when they admitted it: the stairs, the fire, the pretence of leisure. They divided the crockery amicably — she took the green cups, he took the plates — and gave up the lease.

Two years later she found him in a bar near his office and told him her marriage was finished, and that she had spent the previous night telling Emlyn everything, all of it, the rooms and the linen and the years. She looked exhausted and rather proud. Then, in passing, she mentioned that Emlyn had been publishing that awful man — the one Wilder represented, the one they both privately thought a fraud — for some time now, hadn't Wilder known?

Wilder rang Emlyn that afternoon in a condition he could not name, and Emlyn said he'd come round, and came that same evening, in his overcoat, refusing a drink.

"I've known four years," he said. "She told me in Spain. I'd have mentioned it, but there seemed no occasion." He looked at the fire. "And I never thought much of your letters either."

All night the helicopters went over, low and unhurried, laying their pale fog across the citrus trees and the carports and the flat roofs of the strip malls, spraying for the medfly, and no one woke except the ones who never sleep anyway.

Doctor Neil Hartigan stood in front of the mirror knotting his tie while Bess washed turpentine off her hands, and they said the sort of things people say before a dinner party, about who drinks what, about how long they'd have to stay.

Across town Otto Kemp took a phone order in his flour-dusted apron: a chocolate cake, eight years old, a boy named Charlie Rill, ready Monday afternoon. He wrote the name on a card and set it in the tray with the others.

Charlie never got to the cake. He was walking to school with his lunch bag when Rhona, a waitress running late, clipped him at the crossing and got out shaking, and the boy stood up and said he was fine, he was fine, and walked home and told his mother he was fine. Then he lay down on the couch and did not get up. Elaine and Grant sat in the hospital under the fluorescent hum while machines counted for their son, and on the third day Grant's father Duff came shuffling in, a man Grant had not spoken to in twenty years, and sat down and told him about a woman in 1961, about how he had loved her, as though a coma were a confessional.

Nobody picked up the cake. Nobody paid for it. Otto let the phone ring in his shop and then he began to make the calls himself, late, breathing, saying I have something of yours, saying did you forget about Charlie, and hanging up.

Cheryl worked the sex line from her living room with a basket of laundry between her knees, telling a stranger in a low voice exactly what she was wearing while Stu sat across from her with a beer and a face like a closed fist. Saturday he drove out with Vern and the other two to fish the Kern, and there she was in the shallows, a girl, naked, face down among the stones. They looked at her a long while. Then they tied her ankle to a root with fishing line so she wouldn't drift, and they fished two more days and drank their beer and cooked their trout, and only on the way home did they stop at a phone booth. When Vern told Iris, still in her clown paint from a birthday party, she put down her wig and looked at him as if she had married a stranger.

In the club Vida sang standards in a blue dress until one in the morning, and at home her daughter Bee played cello in an empty house, the same passage again and again.

Officer Rowe was with Nan in the afternoons and with Peg at night, and when a lie needed shoring up he drove the family dog out past the freeway and let it go, and came home and helped his children make posters. Nan's ex-husband Cass flew the spray helicopters, and when he heard she had somebody he let himself into her apartment with a handsaw and cut the couch, the table, the bed frame into pieces, and sat on the floor among them.

Ike and Dot were house-sitting the Hartigans' place, and Dot lay in the bathtub with blue eyeshadow bruises and ketchup at her mouth while Ike photographed her, laughing, for the money in it.

At the dinner party Bess told the story about posing nude for a painter thirty years ago, and then, because of the wine, told the other part too, and Neil stood up so fast his chair went over and asked her in a shout how long, how long, while the guests studied their plates.

Charlie died at 6:20 in the morning. Grant and Elaine drove to the bakery in the dark to scream at the man who had called their house, and Otto Kemp sat them down among the ovens and gave them warm rolls and coffee and talked about being alone with the smell of bread for forty years, and they ate, and they all wept.

Bee found her mother asleep on the couch, still in the blue dress, and did not wake her. She went out to the garage, closed the door, and started the car.

At a picnic in the hills Stu picked up a rock and brought it down on a young woman's head.

Then the ground moved—every window in the city ringing at once—and by evening it was all one bulletin: the tremor, the girl in the river, the girl in the hills, a garage, a boy, a dog still missing.

Then he lay down on the couch and did not get up. Elaine and Grant sat in the hospital under the fluorescent hum while machines counted for their son, and on the third day Grant's father Duff came shuffling in, a man Grant had not spoken to in twenty years, and sat down and told him about a woman in 1961, about how he had loved her, as though a coma were a confessional.

Nobody picked up the cake. Nobody paid for it. Otto let the phone ring in his shop and then he began to make the calls himself, late, breathing, saying I have something of yours, saying did you forget about Charlie, and hanging up.

Cheryl worked the sex line from her living room with a basket of laundry between her knees, telling a stranger in a low voice exactly what she was wearing while Stu sat across from her with a beer and a face like a closed fist. Saturday he drove out with Vern and the other two to fish the Kern, and there she was in the shallows, a girl, naked, face down among the stones. They looked at her a long while. Then they tied her ankle to a root with fishing line so she wouldn't drift, and they fished two more days and drank their beer and cooked their trout, and only on the way home did they stop at a phone booth. When Vern told Iris, still in her clown paint from a birthday party, she put down her wig and looked at him as if she had married a stranger.

In the club Vida sang standards in a blue dress until one in the morning, and at home her daughter Bee played cello in an empty house, the same passage again and again.

Officer Rowe was with Nan in the afternoons and with Peg at night, and when a lie needed shoring up he drove the family dog out past the freeway and let it go, and came home and helped his children make posters. Nan's ex-husband Cass flew the spray helicopters, and when he heard she had somebody he let himself into her apartment with a handsaw and cut the couch, the table, the bed frame into pieces, and sat on the floor among them.

Ike and Dot were house-sitting the Hartigans' place, and Dot lay in the bathtub with blue eyeshadow bruises and ketchup at her mouth while Ike photographed her, laughing, for the money in it.

At the dinner party Bess told the story about posing nude for a painter thirty years ago, and then, because of the wine, told the other part too, and Neil stood up so fast his chair went over and asked her in a shout how long, how long, while the guests studied their plates.

Charlie died at 6:20 in the morning. Grant and Elaine drove to the bakery in the dark to scream at the man who had called their house, and Otto Kemp sat them down among the ovens and gave them warm rolls and coffee and talked about being alone with the smell of bread for forty years, and they ate, and they all wept.

Bee found her mother asleep on the couch, still in the blue dress, and did not wake her. She went out to the garage, closed the door, and started the car.

At a picnic in the hills Stu picked up a rock and brought it down on a young woman's head.

Then the ground moved—every window in the city ringing at once—and by evening it was all one bulletin: the tremor, the girl in the river, the girl in the hills, a garage, a boy, a dog still missing.

He was born in Ilium, where the smoke of the foundries made a kind of weather all its own, and he grew up thin and blinking and strange, a boy who could not throw and could not run and who was, everyone agreed, peculiar. His father, who believed in shortcuts, carried him to the deep end of the YMCA pool and threw him in. He did not swim. He went down and sat on the tiles at the bottom and found it restful there, the light wobbling overhead like something seen through a jar. They pulled him out and he was disappointed, though he did not say so.

The war took him and made him a chaplain's assistant, which is to say a man with no weapon and no purpose and no training worth the name, and shipped him across the ocean into a forest where the line had already broken. He was lost there with a scout, a small furious man who beat him about the head because he wanted only to lie down in the snow and be left. The scout said he was the sorriest excuse for a soldier ever issued. Then they were taken, and put on a train, and the scout's leg turned green and then black, and he died on the straw saying it was all this fool's doing, remember that, remember who did this.

They kept him in a camp next to a barracks of enemy officers who had been drawing double rations for years on account of a clerk's error and who were consequently pink and cheerful and full of songs. Then he was sent on to a beautiful old city and quartered with other prisoners in a slaughterhouse that no longer slaughtered anything. On a night in February the city burned. He was in the meat locker underground with the guards and the carcasses, and in the morning they came up the stairs and the city was gone. It was like the surface of the moon, only warmer. Afterward the prisoners dug in the cellars for bodies, and one of the diggers, an older man, began to heave and could not stop heaving and died of it. And a fellow prisoner, thick-necked, tender in his own way, told him quietly that he would have him killed one day, hire it done, on the scout's account, since somebody had to answer for the scout.

He came home and walked into his mother's kitchen and sat down and did not get up for some weeks. In the veterans' hospital a man in the next bed lent him paperbacks by a hack who wrote about the future, and those books explained the universe to him better than the chaplain ever had. Then he married the daughter of the man who owned the optometry school and became, in the fullness of time, rich. He fitted lenses onto the faces of people who wanted to see better. He had a house and a dog and a swimming pool he never entered.

An airplane carrying optometrists to a convention flew into a mountain in Vermont, and he was the only one who lived. His wife, driving to the hospital in a Cadillac with its exhaust pipe torn away, breathed the fumes all the way there and died in the emergency entrance with the engine still running.

The aliens came for him after that, or perhaps they had already come, since with them the tenses give out. They kept him in a zoo on their planet, in a geodesic dome with furniture from Sears, and gave him a film actress for company, and the two of them were much admired. The aliens explained that every moment simply is, always, permanently, and that the notion of free will was a local eccentricity of Earth, found nowhere else among the hundreds of inhabited worlds. He found this comforting. It excused a great deal.

He went on the radio in New York to tell people about it, about the aliens and the fourth dimension and how nobody ever really dies, and the host went to a commercial. His daughter decided he was senile and took the checkbook and the house and the driving away from him.

He knew how it ended because he had already seen it. He spoke to a crowd about time, and a man with a beam weapon shot him dead, exactly on schedule, and he was elsewhere at the bottom of a bright pool, resting.
